package_info.package_versions: All known versions (Win32/Spacecolon.A, Win64/Spacecolon.A, Win64/DelShad.D, Win32/Filecoder.FS, Win32/Filecoder.Spacecolon.A)
package_info.why_malicious: Spacecolon is a modular toolset attributed to the CosmicBeetle threat actor, designed to facilitate unauthorized access, maintain persistence, deploy ransomware (Scarab, ScRansom), and exfiltrate data from compromised Windows systems. It provides remote access, executes arbitrary commands, disables security products, and delivers ransomware without user consent. Its components (ScHackTool, ScInstaller, ScService, ransomware payloads, and shadow copy deletion utility) are engineered for post-exploitation, lateral movement, and destructive payload delivery, making it a comprehensive threat to enterprise environments.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ScHackTool loads and executes third-party tools to disable security products, extract credentials, and escalate privileges. It can deploy additional payloads (ScInstaller, ScService) and execute arbitrary commands received from the operator.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After initial compromise, the code executes as a service or process, loads and runs red team tools (such as credential dumpers and AV killers), deploys further payloads (including ScInstaller and ScService), and enables lateral movement and persistence by executing arbitrary commands from the operator.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The orchestrator's ability to load and execute arbitrary third-party hacking tools, disable security controls, and deploy additional malware components is highly indicative of a post-exploitation framework used by threat actors for further compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate administrative tools do not covertly deploy malware, disable security controls, or execute arbitrary commands from remote operators without explicit user knowledge and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red team frameworks in authorized penetration tests may use similar orchestration capabilities, but only with explicit authorization and in controlled environments.
key_indicators: Execution of multiple third-party hacking tools from non-standard locations
Deployment of additional malware components (e.g., ScInstaller, ScService)
Disabling of security products and services
Ability to execute arbitrary commands received remotely

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ScInstaller installs ScService as a persistent Windows service, configuring it to start automatically and run with elevated privileges.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When executed on demand, the code writes the ScService binary to disk, registers it as a Windows service, sets it to auto-start with elevated privileges, and ensures persistence for remote access by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Installing unauthorized services for persistence, especially those configured to auto-start and run with elevated privileges, is a common tactic used by malware to maintain long-term access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers do not install backdoor services or configure persistent unauthorized services without user consent and clear documentation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise software may install services, but only with user approval, clear documentation, and legitimate business justification.
key_indicators: Silent installation of a backdoor service (ScService)
Auto-start configuration of the installed service
No user notification or consent during installation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: ScService acts as a backdoor, connecting to C&C servers, executing commands, downloading and running payloads, and collecting system information.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At service start and during runtime, the code establishes outbound connections to hardcoded C&C domains, receives and executes arbitrary commands from the attacker, downloads and executes additional malware payloads, and exfiltrates system and user data to remote servers.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Backdoor functionality with persistent C&C communication, arbitrary command execution, payload delivery, and data exfiltration is a hallmark of remote access trojans and advanced persistent threats.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate services do not connect to unknown C&C servers, execute arbitrary remote commands, or exfiltrate sensitive data without explicit user authorization.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote management tools may have similar features, but only in trusted, managed environments with proper authentication and oversight.
key_indicators: Outbound connections to known malicious C&C infrastructure
Ability to download and execute further payloads on demand
Exfiltration of system and user data

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Ransomware payload encrypts user files, appends custom extensions, and drops ransom notes demanding payment for decryption.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When executed on demand, the code enumerates files on local and network drives, encrypts them using strong cryptography, renames files with a new extension, and creates ransom notes in affected directories to demand payment for decryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: File encryption combined with ransom note creation and payment demands are definitive behaviors of ransomware, designed to extort victims and cause operational disruption.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate software should encrypt user files and demand payment for decryption; such actions are inherently malicious and violate user trust.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or security software may encrypt files for protection, but never for extortion or without user control and transparency.
key_indicators: Mass file encryption across local and network drives
Creation of ransom notes in affected directories
File extension changes to custom values
Demand for payment to restore access

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Deletes Windows Shadow Copies to prevent file recovery after ransomware encryption.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Before or during ransomware execution, the code issues system commands to delete all Volume Shadow Copies, removing backup restore points and preventing file recovery after encryption.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Systematic deletion of shadow copies is a well-known anti-recovery tactic in ransomware attacks, intended to maximize the impact and force victims to pay the ransom.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not delete all system backups or restore points without explicit user consent and clear justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup management tools may delete old shadow copies, but only with user approval and in accordance with retention policies.
key_indicators: Systematic deletion of all shadow copies via system commands
Action occurs immediately before or during file encryption

attack_chain.action: Initial compromise of target system via ZeroLogon exploit or RDP brute force.
Deployment and execution of ScHackTool to orchestrate further actions and deploy additional tools.
attack_chain.leads_to: Disabling security, credential extraction, and deployment of ScInstaller

attack_chain.action: Installation of ScService for persistent remote access.
ScService connects to C&C, executes commands, downloads payloads, and exfiltrates data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransomware deployment or further lateral movement

attack_chain.action: Deployment of ransomware payload (Scarab/ScRansom) to encrypt files and demand ransom.
Deletion of Windows Shadow Copies to prevent recovery.
attack_chain.leads_to: Irreversible data loss unless ransom is paid

behavioral_signatures: Execution of unknown PE files named app.exe, ap.exe, Taskmgr.exe, a.exe, installer.exe, svcss.exe, svvc.exe, 1new.exe, kkk.exe, Project1.exe, Shadow.exe
Installation of unauthorized Windows services with auto-start from non-standard file paths
Outbound connections to known Spacecolon C&C domains or IP addresses
Mass file encryption activity and creation of ransom notes in user directories
Systematic deletion of Volume Shadow Copies via system commands (e.g., vssadmin delete shadows)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of suspicious PE files matching known Spacecolon component names and hashes, especially from non-standard directories. Detect unauthorized installation of Windows services, particularly those set to auto-start and running from unusual file paths. Alert on outbound connections to known Spacecolon C&C domains and IPs. Look for mass file encryption activity, creation of ransom notes in user directories, and systematic deletion of shadow copies using system utilities. Correlate these behaviors to identify the full attack chain and block further malicious activity.
